issues.legal_issue: Multiple principals may jointly appoint one agent by a power of attorney.
material_facts: Three principals jointly executed a power of attorney appointing one agent.
No provision of contract law or general contract law was shown to make their joint appointment impermissible.
issues.conclusion: The joint appointment was legally permissible.
issues.legal_principle: An agency arises when an agent has authority to act on behalf of a principal and consents to do so; co-principals may jointly appoint an agent. The Court agreed with the proposition stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England, Fourth Edition, Volume 1, paragraph 726.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.multiple_principals_jointly_appointed_on: Multiple principals jointly appointed one agent to act on their behalf.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal concerns a joint appointment made by multiple principals, the appointment is permissible.

issues.legal_issue: A power of attorney executed jointly by co-principals may authorize the agent to deal with each principal’s individual property when its terms and the circumstances show that this was the intended scope.
material_facts: The principals had separate lands and no evidence showed that they owned joint property or carried on a joint business or venture.
They faced difficulty accessing or managing their respective lands and executed one power of attorney for convenience.
The instrument authorized the agent to act on their behalf, and the circumstances showed that each principal intended the agent to deal with that principal’s property.
issues.conclusion: The power of attorney was not confined to joint affairs or jointly owned property; it authorized the agent to act in respect of each principal’s individual property.
issues.legal_principle: A power of attorney is ordinarily construed strictly: Bryant, Powis and Bryant Ltd. v. La Banque du Peuple, [1893] A.C. 170 at 177. Its scope depends on its terms and purpose, and surrounding circumstances may be considered to ascertain the parties’ intention: Modi & Co. v. Union of India. The instrument must be considered as a whole.

rule.if: civil_appeal and jointly_executed_agency_document and principals_owned_separate_property and circumstances_show_individual_property_purpose

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.jointly_executed_agency_document: Multiple principals jointly executed an instrument appointing an agent.
predicates.principals_owned_separate_property: The principals had separate property rather than only property held jointly.
predicates.circumstances_show_individual_property_p: The circumstances showed that the principals appointed the agent so that each could have their individual property managed or dealt with.

issues.definition: When co-principals jointly appoint an agent and the circumstances show that they intended the agent to deal with their separate properties, the authority extends to each principal’s individual property.

issues.legal_issue: An express power to sell land authorizes the agent to sell agricultural as well as non-agricultural land, without an unstated restriction tying the sale to financing litigation or repaying a loan.
material_facts: The power of attorney expressly authorized the agent to purchase and sell land and execute and register sale deeds.
A supplemental instrument confirmed the power to sell and register sale deeds.
The instruments stated the power to sell separately from powers concerning litigation and borrowing.
The lands at issue included agricultural land.
issues.conclusion: The power of attorney authorized the sale of the lands, including agricultural land, and the authority was not restricted to sales for financing litigation or repaying a loan.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied strict construction of a power of attorney while giving effect to the instrument’s express and unambiguous terms. The document must be read as a whole; an ordinary authority given in one part is not cut down by ambiguous or uncertain expressions elsewhere. The Court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England, Fourth Edition, Volume 1, paragraph 733, and held that “lands” includes agricultural and non-agricultural land.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.agency_document_expressly_authorizes_lan: The principals’ agency document expressly authorized the agent to sell land.
predicates.sale_power_is_stated_independently_of_ot: The instrument stated the power to sell separately from powers concerning litigation, borrowing, or other matters.

issues.definition: When an agency document expressly and independently authorizes land sales, the agent may sell land, including agricultural land, without an unstated restriction based on the document’s other powers.

issues.legal_issue: An owner who consents to another person holding themselves out as owner and acquiesces in a transfer for consideration cannot later challenge the transfer on the ground that the apparent owner lacked authority.
material_facts: The owner’s father acted as though he owned the land and entered into an agreement to sell it before the power of attorney was executed.
The sale was completed by the agent under the power of attorney.
The owner was present when consideration was paid and accepted it.
The owner later challenged the sale, including on the ground that the agent merely completed a transaction negotiated by another person.
issues.conclusion: The owner was estopped from challenging the sale on the ground that the apparent owner lacked authority or that the agent merely executed the prior agreement; the transfer was protected under the principle codified in Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that a transfer for consideration by an ostensible owner is not voidable for lack of authority where the person interested in the property expressly or impliedly consented to that person’s being ostensible owner. The Court relied on the equitable principle stated in Ramcoomar v. Macqueen (1872) I.A. 11 Bengal L.R. 46.

rule.if: civil_appeal and apparent_owner_held_out_with_owner_consent and transfer_for_consideration and owner_acquiesced_in_transfer

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.apparent_owner_held_out_with_owner_conse: A person acted as the owner of property with the express or implied consent of the person interested in it.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The apparent owner’s transfer of the property was made for consideration.
predicates.owner_acquiesced_in_transfer: The person interested in the property knew of and acquiesced in the transaction, including by accepting its consideration.

issues.definition: When an apparent owner acts with the interested person’s consent and transfers property for consideration with that person’s acquiescence, the interested person cannot challenge the transfer for the apparent owner’s lack of authority.

issues.legal_issue: Omission of an endorsement identifying the executants does not invalidate a power of attorney when the executants admit execution and no rule requires the endorsement.
material_facts: The registration endorsement did not state that the executants were personally known to the registering officer or identified by someone known to that officer.
The executants admitted that they had executed the instrument.
No rule or regulation requiring that endorsement was identified.
A general power of attorney was not a compulsorily registrable document.
issues.conclusion: The omission did not invalidate the power of attorney.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that failure to record that the executants were known to or identified before the registering officer does not invalidate the instrument where execution is admitted. It also noted that a general power of attorney is not compulsorily registrable and that no rule or regulation requiring the endorsement had been shown.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.executants_admit_execution: The persons who executed the instrument admitted that they had done so.
predicates.identification_endorsement_omitted: The registering officer’s endorsement did not state that the executants were known to the officer or identified by someone known to the officer.
predicates.no_mandatory_endorsement_rule_shown: No rule or regulation requiring the omitted endorsement was shown.

issues.definition: When the executants admit execution and no rule requiring an identification endorsement is shown, omission of that endorsement does not invalidate the instrument.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence when it requires the evidence to pronounce judgment or another substantial cause exists, and a proper exercise of that discretion will not be disturbed merely because the evidence was not produced at trial.
material_facts: The trial court awarded possession of certain lands because sale deeds had not been produced.
The appellate court admitted registered sale deeds under Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, giving reasons for considering them necessary to decide the appeal.
The appellate court relied on the deeds in allowing the appeal of the affected defendants.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court properly admitted the sale deeds as additional evidence, and its decision to do so was not to be disturbed; once considered, the deeds defeated the possession decree that had rested only on their non-production.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not give a party a right to produce additional evidence. It does, however, empower the appellate court to admit evidence where it requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. A properly exercised discretionary decision in the interest of justice is not to be interfered with.

predicates.appeal_before_appellate_court: The matter was an appeal before an appellate court.
predicates.appellate_court_requires_additional_evid: The appellate court considered additional evidence necessary to pronounce judgment or necessary for another substantial cause.
predicates.additional_evidence_is_material: The additional evidence was material to deciding the dispute.

issues.definition: When an appellate court needs material additional evidence to decide an appeal or for another substantial cause, it may admit that evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A person named as the holder of granted property is not a benamidar merely because another person may have influenced the grant, where no consideration was provided for the grant.
material_facts: The grant and patta were made in the plaintiff’s name when he was a minor.
The plaintiff’s father was alleged to have been the real owner and to have caused the patta to be issued in the plaintiff’s name.
There was no evidence that consideration was paid or provided for the grant.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was not a benamidar; the contention that he could not claim the property on that basis was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, concerns property transferred to one person for consideration paid or provided by another where the latter did not intend the consideration as a benefit to the transferee. The Court explained that the concept of benami requires consideration to flow from one person for a transfer taken in another person’s name, without an intention to make a gift to that transferee. Those elements were absent for a grant unsupported by evidence of consideration.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.property_granted_in_claimants_name: The property was granted or recorded in the claimant’s name.
predicates.no_consideration_provided_by_another_per: No evidence showed that another person paid or provided consideration for the grant or transfer.

issues.definition: When property is granted in a claimant’s name and no other person provided consideration for it, the claimant is not a benamidar merely because another person may have influenced the grant.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise with some defendants does not make an appeal against other defendants infructuous when the claims against the remaining defendants rest on the scope of the agent’s authority and the title acquired through the agent.
material_facts: The plaintiff compromised with some defendants, including the agent and a person alleged to have participated in the fraud.
The appeal continued against other purchasers.
The suit and appeal also concerned the scope of the power of attorney and whether the other purchasers acquired title through the agent’s exercise of that authority.
issues.conclusion: The compromise did not render the appeal against the remaining defendants infructuous or untenable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a compromise with some defendants does not dispose of independent issues concerning the authority under which other purchasers acquired title; the compromise may have been made for reasons such as recovery of part of the loss.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.compromise_with_some_defendants: The appellant compromised the dispute with some, but not all, defendants.
predicates.independent_title_claims_remain_against_: Claims remain against other defendants concerning whether they acquired title through an agent acting under the disputed authority.

issues.definition: When an appellant compromises with some defendants but independent claims about other defendants’ title remain, the appeal against the remaining defendants survives.
